statement: With stock 13/50 gearing and the stock 120/80-19 rear tire, road speed per 1,000 rpm works out to about 1: 4.3 mph, 2: 5.3 mph, 3: 6.3 mph, 4: 7.5 mph, 5: 8.6 mph. One more tooth on the rear sprocket makes every gear about 2.0% shorter; one less on the front about 8.3% shorter.

vals.gear_1: 4.3 mph (6.9 km/h) per 1,000 rpm; overall ratio 18.36:1
vals.gear_2: 5.3 mph (8.6 km/h) per 1,000 rpm; overall ratio 14.81:1
vals.gear_3: 6.3 mph (10.2 km/h) per 1,000 rpm; overall ratio 12.46:1
vals.gear_4: 7.5 mph (12.1 km/h) per 1,000 rpm; overall ratio 10.49:1
vals.gear_5: 8.6 mph (13.9 km/h) per 1,000 rpm; overall ratio 9.18:1

notes: Worked out from Kawasaki's published primary ratio 2.727, gearbox ratios and final drive 13/50: speed = rpm / (primary x gear x final) x tire circumference. Tire rolling diameter is estimated from the size code (rim 19 in + 2 x 120 mm x 80%) = 675 mm; a knobby under load rolls slightly smaller, so real speeds run a little lower. Multiply by rpm/1,000 for a given engine speed.

vals.gear_1: 3.8 mph (6.2 km/h) per 1,000 rpm; overall ratio 20.66:1
vals.gear_2: 4.8 mph (7.8 km/h) per 1,000 rpm; overall ratio 16.43:1
vals.gear_3: 5.6 mph (9.1 km/h) per 1,000 rpm; overall ratio 14.06:1
vals.gear_4: 7.1 mph (11.3 km/h) per 1,000 rpm; overall ratio 11.25:1
vals.gear_5: 8.8 mph (14.2 km/h) per 1,000 rpm; overall ratio 9.00:1

notes: Worked out from Yamaha's published primary ratio 3.000, gearbox ratios and final drive 14/50: speed = rpm / (primary x gear x final) x tire circumference. notes: Upside-down filter removal per a magazine 2026 first look (Honda text); volume from Honda Australia 2022 data.

topic: exhaust layout change from dual to single
statement: The 2018-2021 engine had two exhaust ports, two headers and two mufflers. From 2022 it has one straight exhaust port, one header routed 74 mm closer to the engine on the right and one muffler, saving 1.7 kg. For 2025 the header and muffler were made straighter again, with internal baffling tuned for torque and an aluminium muffler meeting FIM 109 dB.

vals.2018_2021: dual port, dual header, dual muffler
vals.2022_on: single port, single header and muffler

notes: 2025 details from American Honda 2025 release and Honda Europe 25YM release.

source.name: American Honda: 2022 Honda CRF250RX Features & Benefits

For 2025 the header and muffler were made straighter again, with internal baffling tuned for torque and an aluminium muffler meeting FIM 109 dB.

vals.2022_on: single port, single header and muffler

notes: 2025 details from American Honda 2025 release and Honda Europe 25YM release.

statement: Testers found the 2022-2024 engine quick off the bottom with strong low-to-mid pull and little need for clutch, then falling off after about 8,000 rpm and winding out quickly with an unimpressive top end. notes: Consistent across a magazine 2022 shootout, 2023/2024 race tests and 2024 shootout.

topic: 2020 cam and exhaust changes for low-mid torque
statement: For 2020 Honda attacked the weak low end with an exhaust cam that opens later with less overlap, a reshaped combustion chamber, timing optimised at 8,000 rpm, and mufflers revised for low-mid torque with the header resonator removed. One test of the 2020 found it pulled early, built a strong midrange and kept going into over-rev.
notes: Feel from Australian 2020 review; most US tests still rated the low end weak.

statement: From 2025 the 250 has Honda Selectable Torque Control with three levels plus off. It needs no wheel-speed sensor: when engine rpm rises faster than a set rate it retards ignition and trims fuel injection. Level 1 is lightest and longest, level 3 earliest and strongest for slippery tracks; the last setting is kept at start-up.

vals.method: ignition retard + PGM-FI control on rpm rate of change

notes: Honda Europe calls HSTC new on the 250 for 25YM. A long-term test reports stock setting as level 2 on the green button.

statement: HRC sells a laptop setting tool that adjusts fuel and ignition timing for each throttle opening and rpm point. On 2015-on bikes only the Smooth and Aggressive maps can be edited. notes: Honda Europe 25YM confirms the HRC setting tool tailors the Aggressive and Smooth maps on 2025. Rev limit, launch rpm and HSTC adjustment not mentioned.

statement: The Vortex plug-in ECU sold for 2022-on CRF250R/RX has 10 preset fuel and spark maps and three screwdriver fuel-trim switches (low, mid, high throttle, +12.5% to -10%). With Vortex software, rev limit, enrichment, timing and correction tables can be changed. Sellers claim gains mostly on top with sharper low-end response.
notes: Dealer listing; no measured gains given. A 2026 tester suggested Vortex plus dual injector as the next step but had not tested it.

source.name: CRFsOnly: CRF250R/RX 22-24 Pro Circuit Ti-6 + Vortex ECU combo

statement: A magazine long-term 2025 bike ran a GET ECU (a 2024 unit, since no 2025 version existed) remapped on a dyno with an O2 sensor to about 14:1 air-fuel. The engine liked slightly leaner fuel low and richer high, with more advance low and less as revs rise; hard-pack, mud and sand maps were switchable by Wi-Fi.
notes: No dyno power numbers published in this instalment. Removing the airbox backfire screen and enlarging the airbox-cover hole also sharpened response.

source.name: Australasian Dirt Bike: Long Term Test Bike #2, 2025 Honda CRF250R

statement: Honda's 2021-2026 CRF450R covers two chassis generations on one engine family: an all-new 2021 frame, swingarm and bodywork (2021-2024), then a frame with about 70% new parts plus new linkage and suspension for 2025-2026. The 96 x 62.1 mm Unicam engine dates back to the 2017 redesign and was refined in 2021, 2023 and 2025.
notes: Honda's own history: 2017 ground-up redesign, 2018 electric start, 2019 HRC head + launch control, 2020 HSTC, 2021 new chassis. 2025 frame detail from Honda 2025 Features & Benefits. A new-generation 2027 CRF450R (new engine and frame) is outside this slice.

statement: For 2021 Honda redid everything except the wheels and the engine's core: a new frame 700 g lighter with 20% less lateral rigidity, a narrower swingarm, a hydraulic clutch with 8 plates, a single exhaust replacing the twin mufflers (1.24 kg lighter), a 4.1 L airbox, a 46 mm throttle body with a 60-degree injector, 70 mm slimmer bodywork, and 5 mm more fork stroke. Claimed curb weight fell 1.5 kg to 110.5 kg.
notes: Honda Canada press release, specs marked provisional.

source.name: Honda Canada press release: 2021 Honda CRF450R

statement: Honda steepened the 2021 rake from 27.4 to 27.1 degrees and cut trail from 116 to 114 mm, with a 1,481 mm wheelbase, 336 mm ground clearance (+8 mm) and a seat 10 mm lower at the rear.

statement: For 2023 Honda aimed the engine at low-end torque: the throttle body shrank from 46 to 44 mm, the intake port narrowed, the intake funnel and air boot got longer, the cam and valve springs changed, and the ECU was remapped. Honda claims 10.7% more torque at 5,000 rpm with peak power down 5%. The frame got thicker sections, steel head stays replaced aluminium, and the shock spring went up.
notes: A magazine first look relays Honda Europe press data; shared by R and RX.

statement: On a magazine dyno the 2021 Works Edition made 56.7 hp at 9,600 rpm and 34.8 lb-ft at 7,100 rpm, the most peak power of any 450 tested that year.
notes: A magazine in-house dyno (Dynojet 250i per their 2023 tests). Works Edition variant of the CRF450R.

source.name: Dirt Rider: 2021 Honda CRF450RWE Dyno Test

statement: In a 2021 shootout dyno session the CRF450R made 57.54 hp at 9,500 rpm and 35.8 lb-ft at 7,500 rpm, the highest of five 450s.
notes: A magazine shootout, dyno at a tuner Corona, dyno model not named. Pre-reflash 2021 map.

source.name: Vital MX: 2021 Vital MX 450 Shootout Full Test

statement: On a magazine dyno the 2021 CRF450RX made 53.2 hp at 9,400 rpm and 34.3 lb-ft at 7,000 rpm, about 0.5 hp less but 1.1 lb-ft more than the 2020 RX.
notes: A magazine in-house dyno, Dunlop D404 street tire on rear. The 2021 standard R dyno article body did not render.

source.name: Dirt Rider: 2021 Honda CRF450RX Dyno Test

statement: On a magazine Dynojet the 2022 CRF450R made 53.8 hp at 9,300 rpm and 34.1 lb-ft at 7,200 rpm, third in peak power behind the KTM and GasGas.
notes: A magazine in-house dyno; map not stated (assume standard).

source.name: Dirt Rider: 2022 Honda CRF450R Dyno Test

statement: A different magazine dyno measured the 2022 CRF450R at 58.20 hp at 9,300 rpm and the 2022 Works Edition at 60.01 hp at 9,600 rpm.
notes: A magazine dyno (type not named); figures quoted in its 2023 race test for comparison.

source.name: Motocross Action: MXA Race Test 2023 Honda CRF450

statement: On a magazine Dynojet 250i the 2023 CRF450R made 52.5 hp at 9,100 rpm and 35.1 lb-ft at 6,600 rpm: fifth in peak power but first in peak torque among the 450s tested.
notes: A magazine Dynojet 250i rear-wheel dyno, D404 street tire; map not stated.

source.name: Dirt Rider: 2023 Honda CRF450R Dyno Test

statement: A second magazine dyno measured the 2023 CRF450R at 56.3 hp at 9,100 rpm, with map peaks of 56.88 hp (Standard), 55.97 hp (Smooth) and 56.24 hp (Aggressive). It beat the 2022 from 4,500 to 7,000 rpm, matched it to 8,200 and fell behind above 8,300 rpm.
notes: A magazine dyno, type not named; the headline 56.3 and map peaks are unreconciled in the source.

source.name: Motocross Action: MXA Race Test 2023 Honda CRF450

statement: On a magazine dyno the 2023 CRF450RX made 51.0 hp at 9,300 rpm and 34.1 lb-ft at 6,800 rpm, 2.2 hp and 0.2 lb-ft below the 2021 RX.
notes: A magazine in-house dyno; map not stated.

source.name: Dirt Rider: 2023 Honda CRF450RX Dyno Test

statement: On a magazine Dynojet 250i the 2023 Works Edition made 54.7 hp and 34.7 lb-ft, about 2.2 hp more and 0.4 lb-ft less than the standard 2023 bike.
notes: A magazine Dynojet 250i, D404 tire. Works Edition variant.

source.name: Dirt Rider: How much power does the 2023 Honda CRF450RWE make?

statement: A magazine dyno measured the 2024 CRF450R at 56.9 hp at 9,100 rpm in the Standard map; the Smooth map gave up about 1 hp across the range and the Aggressive map made less power everywhere.
notes: A magazine dyno, type not named. Smooth figure repeats the 2023 number exactly.

source.name: Motocross Action: MXA Race Test 2024 Honda CRF450

statement: On a magazine dyno the 2025 CRF450R made 51.1 hp and 32.9 lb-ft, not the peak leader but praised for one of the most usable deliveries in the class.
notes: A magazine in-house dyno; rpm and map not stated.

source.name: Dirt Rider: How much power does the 2025 Honda CRF450R make?

source.name: Motocross Action: MXA Race Test 2025 Honda CRF450

statement: On a magazine dyno the 2025 CRF450RX made 52.1 hp and 34.5 lb-ft, 1.1 hp and 0.4 lb-ft more than the previous RX.
notes: A magazine in-house dyno; same dyno read the 2025 R at 51.1 hp.

source.name: Dirt Rider: How much power does the 2025 Honda CRF450RX make?

statement: On a magazine dyno the 2025 Works Edition made 54.6 hp and 34.4 lb-ft, out-pulling the standard bike from 3,000-3,400 rpm and from 4,200 rpm to the roughly 11,500 rpm limit.

source.name: Dirt Rider: How much power does the 2025 Honda CRF450RWE make?

statement: On a tuner's dyno in a 12-bike shootout the CRF450R made 55.3 hp at 8,700 rpm and 36.5 lb-ft at 7,000 rpm: mid-to-low on peak power but tied for the most torque, with the lowest power-peak rpm of all twelve.
notes: A magazine shootout on a tuner dyno (model not named), standard map, air-density corrected. Published Nov 2025, assumed MY2026 (2026 = 2025 carry-over).

notes: Engineering reasoning from published Honda changes (a magazine/Honda Europe data); matches the magazine dyno shift of torque peak from 7,200 to 6,600 rpm.

statement: Honda Selectable Torque Control has three levels plus off. It has no wheel-speed sensor: when engine rpm rises faster than a threshold it retards ignition and trims fuel. Level 1 intervenes lightest and latest, Level 2 is in between, Level 3 is quickest and strongest for slippery or muddy tracks.
notes: Button on left switch, hold 0.5 s to cycle; green LED flashes 1-3 times; last setting restored at start-up.

statement: The 2024 head traded the 40 mm intake valves for 38 mm ones and a straighter, steeper port, and the rod got 5 mm longer, which favours smooth, broad delivery over hit; the small airbox, the factory rubber plug and a restrictive stock muffler add to the soft throttle response that testers report.
notes: BAK reasoning from Kawasaki's architecture changes plus magazine observations that intake and stock exhaust are the main limits (a magazine exhaust test) and that opening the airbox improves response. Not a manufacturer statement.

statement: Engine tuners commonly build a KX250 map that combines the white coupler's ignition with the black coupler's fuel; it adds modest midrange torque and carries power further up the rpm range.
notes: Requires the calibration kit to build.

vals.monitoring: rpm, TPS, intake pressure, coolant temp, air temp, ignition offset

notes: KX450 from 2024, KX250 from 2025. The app does not show engine hours (magazine complaint).

statement: The mid-2022 KTM 250 SX-F Factory Edition was the first bike with the new engine and frame: 81 x 48.5 mm, compression up from 14.4 to 14.5:1, exhaust valves up from 26.5 to 27.5 mm, a lighter head, engine tilted 2 degrees back, 8 mm shorter engine, 3 mm lower countershaft sprocket, 22 mm rear axle (was 25 mm), new WP shock and quickshift.

notes: Valve sizes also in KTM 250 XC-F press text. Weight rose from 218 lb (2022) to 224-226 lb depending on scale.

statement: For 2025 the frame kept its geometry but lost material for more flex: relief holes in the forged shock tower, hollowed head stays, thinner backbone plates and thinner-wall long tubes. The linkage arms got shorter and thinner with smaller bolts (17 to 15 mm and 17 to 14 mm), shock valving got slightly stiffer with low-stiction seals, the swingarm top was lowered with a raised buffer pad, traction control was improved and the rear brake pedal tip was strengthened.
notes: 2023-2024 aftermarket linkages do not fit 2025. 2024 radiator graphics do not fit 2025 shrouds. Testers felt the softer frame most in acceleration chop. A magazine says KTM did not announce any mapping changes.

topic: why it feels the way it does
statement: The short 48.5 mm stroke, light finger-follower valvetrain and big titanium valves let the engine breathe and rev to 14,000 rpm. Peak torque arrives around 9,200-9,600 rpm but peak power not until about 13,000-13,500 rpm, so power keeps rising for over 4,000 rpm after the torque peak. On the YZ250F that gap is under 2,800 rpm, which is why the Yamaha feels punchy and then signs off while the KTM feels flat but keeps pulling.
notes: Gap computed from the 2025 a tuner dyno figures (a magazine): KTM 13,470 - 9,210 = 4,260 rpm; YZ250F 12,880 - 10,100 = 2,780 rpm. Architecture explanation combines KTM data (finger followers, valve sizes, 14,000 rpm) with testers' descriptions; the link between them is BAK's engineering reading.

vals.arming: TC + QS buttons together at idle

notes: The 30% figure comes from a magazine describing a 2017 KTM; not confirmed for the 2023+ system. Testers rarely use launch control on dirt starts but do on concrete.

statement: Adding one tooth to the rear sprocket gives more low-rpm pull for riders who do not like to rev the engine; riders who stay high in the revs may not need it.

statement: For 2023 KTM changed nearly everything: new hydroformed chromoly frame with a forged shock mount and reworked stiffness, engine rotated 2 degrees back so the countershaft sprocket sits 3 mm lower, higher compression, new airbox, hollow die-cast swingarm, shorter and lighter WP XACT shock (15 mm shorter, about 100 g lighter), fork Hydrostops, quickshifter, and bigger die-cast footpegs moved inward.
notes: Shock length/weight from a magazine 2023 race test; footpeg size from a magazine; rest from a magazine First Look (KTM press data).

source.name: Motocross Action: First Look 2023 KTM 450SXF/350SXF/250SXF

statement: The 2023 450 SX-F Factory Edition (released mid-season) added an Akrapovic slip-on, factory triple clamps, an orange frame, factory seat and wheels, semi-floating front disc, Hinson clutch cover, holeshot device, vented airbox cover and gold chain. Price was $12,099.
notes: A magazine bike guide listing (manufacturer data).

source.name: Vital MX bike guide: 2023 KTM 450 SX-F Factory Edition

statement: 2024 was a carry-over year: new graphics with purple accents, fork and shock valving taken from the 2023.5 Factory Edition, shock high-speed compression shim stack grown from 15 to 23 shims for finer adjustment, a better-sealed start/stop switch, and a one-piece air inlet sleeve/snorkel. MSRP $11,099.
notes: A magazine race test (magazine reporting of KTM changes); one-piece snorkel listed in a magazine 2024 FE guide.

source.name: Motocross Action: MXA Race Test 2024 KTM 450SXF

statement: The 2025 450 SX-F got the Factory Edition frame (cut-outs and thinner walls at the head tube, engine mounts and shock tower, about 300 g lighter), shorter and slimmer shock linkage arms with smaller bolts and new seals, reworked fork settings, revised shock geometry for more linkage ground clearance, a swingarm with a lowered top and thicker/machined chain slider, a new silencer, new bi-composite tank shrouds, a one-piece stiffer air inlet sleeve, a stronger rear brake pedal, a new chain guide, and Dunlop Geomax MX34 tyres.
notes: Combined from KTM model page, a magazine/Bikesales range reports and a magazine tech page (MSRP).

source.name: KTM 2025 450 SX-F model page

statement: Testers report that 2025 engine changes were mostly ECU, quickshifter, throttle-body and reliability tweaks plus a new silencer that KTM says sharpens response with the map switch and is slightly quieter; the quickshifter gained two reaction speeds.
notes: A magazine describes the changes without part-level detail; KTM page confirms silencer claim.

source.name: Motocross Action: MXA Race Test 2025 KTM 450SXF

statement: 2026 changes were minimal: a threaded radiator cap that opens with less force, a protection cap on the CPC fuel connector, new graphics, and (per a magazine) a black powder-coated frame and black seat. MSRP $11,649.
notes: A magazine First Look 2026 lists the frame colour; a magazine lists price and changes.

source.name: Dirt Rider: 2026 KTM 450 SX-F Technical Overview

statement: KTM calls the 2027 450 SX-F largely unchanged: in-mould graphics with red, re-routed wiring harness with new fixing points to reduce wear, unspecified engine updates for rideability and to meet the latest FIM/AMA sound rules, and frame wording about shock-mount, engine-mount and wall-thickness optimisation. US bikes arrive late spring 2026.
notes: The frame text may repeat the 2025 frame description rather than describe a new frame; no 2027 dyno or test data found yet.

notes: Later, some tuners offered stock-ECU remaps (see community records).

topic: aftermarket ECU: AIM Taipan and Vortex
statement: A tester preferred an AIM Taipan ECU: per-gear mapping gave a longer-pulling second gear, smoother low end and stronger mid-to-top with better exit traction. A Vortex unit mapped with a tuner also beat stock. Both let him ride a gear higher with less engine braking.
notes: No dyno numbers published.

source.name: Keefer Inc. Testing: 2023 KTM 450 SX-F suspension baseline / chassis tips

statement: Owners report tuners reprogramming Vortex units for 2023+ KTMs (about $1,100 from a tuner), a tuner remaps of stock ECUs, and that older Vortex units may not support the stock map switch, traction control or quickshift. One tuner reportedly said it cannot work on 2023+ ECUs.
notes: A magazine threads Jan 2025 and Nov 2025-Jan 2026; mostly 350 SX-F owners, same ECU family. Results mixed.

statement: KTM sets the 2025 450 SX-F air fork at 10.5 bar (152 psi) for US bikes and 10.4 bar (151 psi) for EU/BR bikes, for a standard rider of 75-85 kg (165-187 lb). Change it in 0.2 bar (3 psi) steps, staying within 7-12 bar (102-174 psi).
notes: KTM's manual gives one standard pressure plus the step size, not a pressure-by-weight table. Set cold, before riding.

topic: 2024 450 SX-F Factory Edition fork oil-height setup
statement: On the 2024 Factory Edition one tester raised fork oil from 240 to 250 ml and dropped air to 10.2 bar (10.3 if landings feel soft), with compression 10 out and rebound 16 out. topic: fork travel indicator: when to change air
statement: Use the fork's rubber travel ring: if it is pushed all the way down after a ride, add a couple of psi; if it stops more than 3 inches from the bottom, lower the pressure. If the fork bottoms at stock pressure, first try a couple of clicks more compression; on doubt about compression, change shock high-speed compression first.
notes: Same article gives the race settings already held in k45-098 (158/152/145/138 psi expert/intermediate/vet/novice; shock 45 N/mm for 175 lb and up, 42 N/mm under 175 lb, 105 mm sag). Tier MEASURED used for magazine test-rider practice; it is a method, not a measurement.

topic: tuner revalve and linkage for faster riders (2021-2022)
statement: One aftermarket tuner's package for the AER-fork 450 SX-F adds a stiffer mid-valve and a low-speed stack in place of the stock bleed hole (more initial control and hold-up), a bladder conversion for the shock (less friction, more nitrogen volume), and a linkage that is softer early and ramps up deeper. It fixed a setup that was too soft for fast riders on rough tracks, at some cost to initial plushness.
notes: Previous-generation frame (2019-2022). The linkage needs a stiffer shock spring. No settings published.

topic: swingarm pivot torque and chain slack
statement: Lowering the swingarm pivot bolt torque to 95 Nm reduces side-to-side deflection over braking and acceleration bumps; use blue thread-lock or check the nut often. Keeping chain slack at 65-70 mm (a figure attributed to KTM development) lets the suspension move freely.
notes: The same pivot-torque trick is held for the 350 in k35-080; the 2025 350 baseline repeats it and says it also applies to Husqvarna and GasGas.

topic: junior race setup, deep loam (130 lb)
statement: A 130 lb (without gear) 15-year-old amateur raced a revalved 250 SX-F in deep loam with the fork at 10 bar, compression 15, rebound 11, 5 mm height, and the shock at 104 mm sag, LSC 12, HSC 1.25, rebound 12. Raising air to 10 bar cut fork dive on deceleration; HSC was then turned in 1/8 turn because the rear sat low on acceleration. Gearing went from 14/51 to 14/52 for the deep dirt.
notes: Previous-generation 250 SX-F with custom-valved suspension (tuner spec codes), so clickers do not transfer directly to stock. An FMF 4.1 system gave stronger low end and weaker top end than the stock exhaust.

source.name: Keefer Inc. Tested - The Weekend Race Set Up (Fox Raceway amateur day)

statement: For 175-200 lb riders: fork 10.8 bar, 2-3 mm up, compression 14 out, rebound 15-16 out. Shock: 103 mm sag, LSC 12 out, HSC 1.5 turns out, rebound 16 out. Lower the swingarm pivot torque to 95 Nm. Allow 6-8 hours of suspension break-in.
notes: Fork sits 2 mm lower than the 2024 baseline (5 mm). Not valid for the Husqvarna FC 350, which has different suspension specs.

source.name: Keefer Inc. Tested - 2025 KTM 350 SX-F Baseline Suspension Settings

topic: sand setting from the KTM app (85 kg B rider)
statement: An owner reported that the KTM app's sand setting for an 85 kg intermediate (B) rider is fork 10.7 bar (about 155 psi), compression 5 clicks, rebound 14, fork tubes with no rings showing, and shock LSC 8, HSC 1 turn, rebound 8.
notes: Second-hand report of KTM app output, not checked against the app. Sag not given; posters advise against sag as low as 98 mm in sand.

source.name: Vital MX - '22 AER48 KTM 350 SXF clickers/fork air for deep sand tracks

statement: Owners on deep sand: a 200 lb C rider dropped from 152 to 140 psi with compression in the mid-20s out, then added about 4 psi, 2-4 clicks of compression and raised sag to 103-105 mm for sand. A 150 lb GasGas MC 350F rider ran 140 psi, compression 14 out, HSC 1.75, LSC 15 and 104 mm sag. Several riders run 105-110 mm sag at sand tracks to ride on top of the sand.

vals.200lb_C_fork: 140 psi, comp 26-28 out; sand +4 psi, +2-4 clicks
vals.150lb_MC350F: 140 psi, comp 14 out, HSC 1.75, LSC 15, sag 104 mm

notes: Several agreeing rider reports, Feb-Mar 2023, on 2021-2022 AER-fork bikes. Opening HSC to 2 turns made the GasGas wallow under acceleration but helped square edges.

topic: heavier rider shock spring on FC 350
statement: For a 190 lb C rider on a stock FC 350 (42 N/mm shock spring, 154 psi fork), owners suggested going up one step to 45 N/mm, or even 48 N/mm.
notes: Suggestions only; no tested outcome reported.

source.name: Vital MX - FC 350 air fork base settings

topic: heavier rider shock spring on FC 350
statement: For a 190 lb C rider on a stock FC 350 (42 N/mm shock spring, 154 psi fork), owners suggested going up one step to 45 N/mm, or even 48 N/mm.
notes: Suggestions only; no tested outcome reported.

source.name: Vital MX - FC 350 air fork base settings

statement: Owners commonly set air so the fork stops about 1 to 1.5 inches from bottoming on the biggest regular hits (checked with a zip tie or O-ring), then tune with clickers and leave the air alone; aim for 103-105 mm shock sag. A rider of 245-255 lb with gear chose a 5.8 kg/mm shock spring.

vals.heavy_rider_spring: 5.8 kg/mm (~57 N/mm) at 245-255 lb with gear

notes: Thread Oct 2024. Spring units as posted (kg/mm, from an aftermarket chart: 5.4 for 231-254 lb, 5.8 for 254-276 lb); the poster did not say which bike the chart covers. Posters note that the 2025 engine mounts can be fitted to 2023-2024 bikes for about $80, and that a shock-linkage knuckle change lets the shock run softer compression without bottoming.

statement: For 170-190 lb riders: fork 10.7 bar, compression 14 out, rebound 14 out, 4-5 mm up. Shock 45 N/mm, 103 mm sag, LSC 10-11 out, HSC 1.25 out, rebound 11-12 out. Over 185 lb, fit a 48 N/mm spring and run LSC 15 out, HSC 1.5 out, rebound 12 out.
notes: Motocross, including loamy and sandy tracks.

source.name: Keefer Inc. Tested - 2023 KTM 300SX Baseline Settings

statement: Magazine race setup: fork 10.5 bar (154 psi), compression 12 out (16 for slower or lighter riders), rebound 12 out (14 for slower riders), second line. Shock 45 N/mm (riders under 155 lb or over 190 lb may need another spring), HSC 1.5 turns out (stock 2), LSC 14 out, rebound 14 out, 105 mm race sag. Testers raced in the full power-valve map (map 2).
notes: Setting method: bleed both fork caps, set sag, then adjust air with a zip tie until the fork stops about 1.5 in from bottoming; recheck on hot days. 150 lb testers could have used 42 N/mm.

source.name: Motocross Action - Race Test 2023 KTM 300SX

topic: exhaust and setup changes on the TBI 300 SX
statement: On the 2023 300 SX one tester found an aftermarket pipe and silencer gave the most mid-range torque and a strong top end, while another popular pipe with its matching silencer gave good response and low end but a flatter top. Going from 13/49 to 13/50 improved third-gear roll-on in loose dirt, and the closed airbox side cover gave crisper throttle response on that bike.

vals.best_pipe: Bills pipe + silencer: most mid-range, strong top
vals.alternative: FMF Fatty + 2.1: good low end, flatter top

notes: Track impressions, no dyno. ECU was locked at the time. FMF dyno numbers for this pipe are in k2t-068.

source.name: Keefer Inc. Tested - 2023 KTM 300SX Baseline Settings

topic: ECU remap for TBI 250 SX / 300 SX
statement: A $349.50 remap of the locked stock ECU keeps the easy, luggable bottom end but sharpens throttle response and adds mid-to-top pull so the engine stops hitting the rev limiter. On a 300 SX with an aftermarket pipe and the stock silencer, a second map let riders use third gear in tight corners.
notes: No dyno numbers published for the remap. Previously a Vortex ignition was needed to remap these bikes. Stock figures are from the magazine's 2024 race test, not labelled as dyno results. Vets preferred the white (80% power valve) map, pros the green (full) map.

source.name: Motocross Action - Team Tested: Twisted Development KTM 250/300 remapped ECU

topic: 125 SX TBI fuel, maps and pipe
statement: The 2024 125 SX runs 40:1 premix on 91-octane pump fuel. The green map is richer, for deep sand, hard use or detonation, but bogged at random on the test bike, so testers used the white map. An aftermarket pipe made detonation worse even on race fuel, so it needs a remap.
notes: The magazine's dyno showed identical curves to about 10,800 rpm. Dyno type not stated. A 150 cc big-bore kit was available in PowerParts.

source.name: Motocross Action - Race Test 2024 KTM 125SX

topic: owner ECU reflash on TBI 250/300 SX
statement: Owners report having 2023 250 SX ECUs flashed with KTM's latest (2025) maps, and a 300 SX flashed after about 40 hours for a smoother hit; others pair a high-compression head insert with an aftermarket pipe. Several say the TBI 250 makes less power and weighs more than the 2022 carbureted 250 SX.
notes: Forum reports, June and December 2025. No dyno numbers.

source.name: Vital MX - KTM SX 250 2025 vs 2022

source.name: Dirt Bike Magazine - 2024 KTM two- and four-stroke cross-country models, new WP spring fork

statement: Testers ran about 105-106 mm sag with the spring fork flush (more stable) or at the stock second line (better cornering). The fork felt softer than the shock, so the bike pitched under hard braking and blew through on big hits; stock valving is soft for an average rider. Gearing 14/52 (stock 14/47) made third usable in corners.
notes: Southern California trails, East Coast-style woods and intermediate desert speeds; rider weights not given. Suggested upgrades: medium-flex engine mounts, 23.5 mm clamps, revalve and springs for weight.

source.name: Dirt Bike Test - 2024 KTM 350 XC-F Review

statement: A trail build ran revalved stock suspension at 105 mm sag with forks flush, which gave controlled, comfortable slow-speed bump absorption and only occasional controlled bottoming. Gearing went to 14/49 (stock 14/47) for more low-end, with a shorter 250F header, aftermarket silencer and custom ECU map for cleaner running and less stalling.
notes: Discipline: single track and off-road loops. Rider weight not given. The 450 SX-F clutch master cylinder reduced clutch fade.

source.name: Dirt Bike Test - Tuned: 2024 KTM 350 XC-F project bike

statement: Testers found the 2026 450 XC-F spring fork softer and lower-riding than the rear, giving a nose-down feel. It is comfortable and controlled at slow speed but bottoms in fast terrain; the setup suits hare scrambles best, and some testers still prefer the older air fork.
notes: No clicker or sag numbers published.

source.name: Dirt Bike Test - First Impression: 2026 KTM 450 XC-F

statement: Riders under about 170 lb needed few clicker changes on the 2024 300 XC-W, but riders over 200 lb found the shock too soft and need stiffer springs. To lift a low front end, run about 110 mm sag rather than moving the fork. Lowering swingarm pivot torque by 5-10% reduces rear stiffness.
notes: Desert and mountain trails. Clicker settings from the same test are in ko2-076.

source.name: Dirt Bike Test - 2024 KTM 300 XC-W Review

statement: The 250 and 300 XC-W used transfer port injection (TPI) with oil injection through 2023; the 150 XC-W got TPI for 2020, replacing its carburetor. For 2024 all three moved to a 39 mm Keihin throttle body (TBI) with an electronic power valve, keeping oil injection.

notes: In Europe the 125/150/250 become XC-W competition models and only the 300 keeps the EXC name (Euro 5+). A fan is standard on the 300 EXC; not listed for the 150/250.

topic: TBI map switch and power valve opening
statement: On the 250/300 TBI off-road bikes map 1 (white, linear) lets the electronic power valve open to only 80%, while map 2 (green, sharper) opens it to 100%; the difference is mostly felt on top and many riders found it hard to notice.
notes: 125 TBI maps change fuel/ignition only (see two_stroke_porting 2t-010). Testers wanted app access to the power valve like Yamaha/Kawasaki.

statement: A long-term TBI 300 XC-W could not reliably pull third gear up steep, sandy high-desert climbs that the TPI bike handled; gearbox ratios are the same, so the difference is the powerband.

statement: Testers found the TBI enduro 300 can crawl at almost closed throttle without stalling, is linear and broader through the mid and top, and no longer coughs or lean-pops after long high-rpm runs as TPI bikes did; older carb bikes still hit harder off the bottom.

statement: The TPI 300 XC shared the XC-W's engine tune: very smooth but lethargic and wheezy off the bottom, with what sounded like low-rpm detonation; race fuel in the mix and a power-valve tool made it livelier.

topic: TPI oil system: no premix, priming
statement: Do not add premix to a TPI oil-injected bike: the oil never reaches the skirts or bearings and has clogged fuel filters. After removing the throttle body, prime the oil line by holding the throttle wide open, plugging in the wake-up dongle for at least 5 seconds, then waiting for the pump clicking to stop.
notes: Reported failures were blamed on dealers not initialising the system, owners not filling the tank, or non-synthetic oil (a magazine Test 2020).

notes: Some testers had pinging on TBI two-strokes using regular premix oil without 50/50 race gas (a magazine Test 2025 EX300).

topic: TBI electronic power valve - no adjuster
statement: TBI bikes replace the centrifugal power valve with an ECU-driven motor set by rpm and throttle position, so there is no rider adjuster; testers find the stock tune conservative and owners report resetting (re-teaching) the valve about every 25-30 hours.
notes: Reset interval is one owner's advice on an SX thread; KTM requires re-teach after cylinder removal (two_stroke_porting 2t-014).

statement: TBI bikes replace the centrifugal power valve with an ECU-driven motor set by rpm and throttle position, so there is no rider adjuster; testers find the stock tune conservative and owners report resetting (re-teaching) the valve about every 25-30 hours.
notes: Reset interval is one owner's advice on an SX thread; KTM requires re-teach after cylinder removal (two_stroke_porting 2t-014).

topic: TPI cold seizure and running hot
statement: The most common TPI seizure comes from riding hard before the engine reaches 175-185 F; the lean stock map also runs hot, and slow first/second-gear climbs can overheat it, so tuners fit a fan set to about 188 F.

topic: how the XC-F differs from the SX-F
statement: The XC-F cross-country bikes use the SX-F motocross engine, frame and electronics but add an 18-inch rear wheel, a bigger fuel tank (2.25 vs 1.9 gal), a kickstand, skid plate, handguards and an O-ring chain, and from 2024 a spring fork instead of the SX-F air fork. Motor, mapping, exhaust and sound level are the same as the SX-F per this test.

vals.fork_2024_on: WP XACT closed-cartridge spring (SX-F: XACT air)

notes: Magazine reporting of KTM spec. 'Unchanged' list (motor, mapping, gear ratios, exhaust, sound, 13-51 gearing) is stated relative to the SX-F for the 450; for 250/350 the XC-F has a 6-speed gearbox instead of the SX-F 5-speed (see drivetrain records).

source.name: Dirt Bike Magazine: Riding the 2025 KTM 450XC-F (The Wrap)

statement: For 2023 the XC-F moved to the new SX-F platform: new cylinder head and crankcases, engine tilted back 2 degrees with the countershaft sprocket 3 mm lower, a die-cast swingarm 190 g lighter, a 22 mm rear axle (old 25 mm wheels will not fit), a 15 mm shorter WP XACT shock, a polyamide/aluminium subframe, a new fuel pump that empties the tank further and compact switches with map, traction control and quickshift buttons. It kept the XACT air fork. The 450 XC-F was $11,649 and weighed 246 lb wet on the magazine scale, 6 lb more than before.
notes: Weight is a magazine measured; most other items are KTM press data reported by a magazine.

statement: For 2024 every XC-F got a WP XACT closed-cartridge spring fork in place of the air fork, with a hydro-stop in the last 68 mm and a new mid-valve piston; travel dropped 10 mm to 300 mm. statement: The 450 XCF-W returned for 2023 as an off-road competition model replacing the emissions-limited 500 XCF-W. Compared with the EXC-F it has no reed valve in the intake boot, no evaporative system, a more open exhaust and its own map. It kept the older (pre-2023) frame with a WP XPLOR coil fork and linkless PDS shock, and cost $11,649.
notes: A magazine 2023 range announcement also describes it as an 'uncorked' version with improved airflow, no airbox reed system, more open exhaust and unique map. Imported as closed-course; not marketed as dual-sport.

statement: For 2024 the 450 XCF-W moved to the new-generation chassis and engine (frame, polyamide subframe and swingarm new, engine tilted 2 degrees back, sprocket 3 mm lower). KTM claims 107.4 kg without fuel; MSRP $11,999.

topic: GasGas EX 2024 changes and differences from MC
statement: For 2024 the GasGas EX got the new frame with an aluminium subframe (KTM/Husqvarna use polyamide hybrids), Braktec brakes, a 9 L tank (+0.5 L) with integrated pump, an 18-inch rear wheel, sidestand, off-road race mapping and a WP XACT closed-cartridge spring fork where the MC has an air fork. The map switch (2 maps, traction control, quickshifter) is an optional accessory, unlike the standard switch on the KTM XC-F.
notes: Combined from GasGas Canada page and a magazine launch report.

notes: A magazine in-house dyno (model not named in this article, Dynojet 250i in others), Dunlop D404 street tyre, stock. Said to equal the 2022 RM-Z450 peak.

source.name: Dirt Rider: 2022 KTM 350 XC-F Dyno Test

statement: On a magazine rear-wheel dyno the 2020 Husqvarna FX 350 made 49.1 hp at 11,700 rpm and 25.5 lb-ft at 8,700 rpm.
notes: A magazine in-house Dynojet 250i, stock bike, fuel and map not stated.

source.name: Dirt Rider: 2020 Husqvarna FX 350 Dyno Test

statement: On a magazine rear-wheel dyno the 2025 Husqvarna FX 350 made 51.0 hp and 27.0 lb-ft.
notes: A magazine in-house Dynojet 250i, stock bike, fuel and map not stated. Rpm points not stated. Tester called it closer to a mellow 450 than a 250F.

source.name: Dirt Rider: 2025 Husqvarna FX 350 Dyno Test

statement: On a magazine rear-wheel dyno the 2020 Husqvarna FX 450 made 51.1 hp at 10,000 rpm and 32.2 lb-ft at 7,600 rpm.
notes: A magazine in-house Dynojet 250i, stock bike, fuel and map not stated.

source.name: Dirt Rider: 2020 Husqvarna FX 450 Dyno Test

statement: On a magazine rear-wheel dyno the 2021 Husqvarna FX 450 made 51.5 hp at 9,300 rpm and 32.9 lb-ft at 7,300 rpm.
notes: A magazine in-house Dynojet 250i, stock bike, fuel and map not stated. D404 street tyre.

source.name: Dirt Rider: 2021 Husqvarna FX 450 Dyno Test

statement: On a magazine rear-wheel dyno the 2023 Husqvarna FX 450 made 53.3 hp at 10,400 rpm and 32.2 lb-ft at 7,500 rpm.
notes: A magazine in-house Dynojet 250i, stock bike, fuel and map not stated. Tester described linear, controllable delivery.

source.name: Dirt Rider: How Much Power Does the 2023 Husqvarna FX 450 Make?

statement: On a magazine rear-wheel dyno the 2021 GasGas EX 350F made 48.9 hp at 11,800 rpm and 25.3 lb-ft at 8,800 rpm.
notes: A magazine in-house Dynojet 250i, stock bike, fuel and map not stated. D404 street tyre; 0.2 hp and 0.2 lb-ft below the 2020 FX 350 per the article.

source.name: Dirt Rider: 2021 GasGas EX 350F Dyno Test

statement: On a magazine rear-wheel dyno the 2021 GasGas EX 250F made 39.3 hp at 13,300 rpm and 18.8 lb-ft at 9,200 rpm. Power and torque dipped clearly between 4,300 and 4,700 rpm on every pull, then rose steeply from 5,300 rpm and stayed linear. It made 1.8 hp less than the 2021 250 SX-F, blamed on no vented airbox cover, no map 2 and the straight header.
notes: A magazine in-house Dynojet 250i, stock bike, fuel and map not stated. No map switch fitted, so map 1 only.

source.name: Dirt Rider: 2021 GasGas EX 250F Dyno Test

statement: On a magazine rear-wheel dyno the 2024 GasGas EX 250F made 41.9 hp and 20.0 lb-ft. The tester described long, linear power with no hard hit that still revs out, which suits the wide-ratio 6-speed.
notes: A magazine in-house Dynojet 250i, stock bike, fuel and map not stated. Rpm points not stated.

source.name: Dirt Rider: 2024 GasGas EX 250F Dyno Test

statement: Worked out from the same magazine dyno, the 2023 450 XCF-W made 6.3 hp (about 12%) and 1.1 lb-ft less than the 2023 450 XC-F, with peak power 300 rpm lower.
notes: 48.3 - 54.6 = -6.3 hp; -6.3/54.6 = -11.5%. 31.9 - 33.0 = -1.1 lb-ft; -1.1/33.0 = -3.3%. 9,200 - 9,500 = -300 rpm. Both a magazine Dynojet 250i 2023; the 2023 XCF-W is the old-generation engine/chassis, so part of the gap may be generation, not just intake/exhaust/map.

source.name: Dirt Rider: 2023 KTM 450 XCF-W Dyno Test

statement: Worked out from the same magazine dyno, the 2023 450 XCF-W made 6.3 hp (about 12%) and 1.1 lb-ft less than the 2023 450 XC-F, with peak power 300 rpm lower.
notes: 48.3 - 54.6 = -6.3 hp; -6.3/54.6 = -11.5%. 31.9 - 33.0 = -1.1 lb-ft; -1.1/33.0 = -3.3%. 9,200 - 9,500 = -300 rpm. Both a magazine Dynojet 250i 2023; the 2023 XCF-W is the old-generation engine/chassis, so part of the gap may be generation, not just intake/exhaust/map.

source.name: Dirt Rider: 2023 KTM 450 XCF-W Dyno Test

statement: Worked out from the same magazine dyno, the 2023 FX 350 made only 2.4 hp less peak power than the FX 450 but 5.4 lb-ft (17%) less torque, peaking 1,000 rpm higher. That matches testers saying the 350 is about 3 hp short of a 450 but needs revs.

source.name: Dirt Rider: How Much Power Does the 2023 Husqvarna FX 350 Make?

statement: Worked out from the same magazine dyno, the 2023 FX 450 made 1.3 hp and 0.8 lb-ft less than the 2023 450 XC-F and peaked 900 rpm higher, despite sharing the engine; the difference is within what unit-to-unit and airbox/exhaust differences can produce.
notes: 53.3-54.6 = -1.3; 32.2-33.0 = -0.8; 10,400-9,500 = +900. Single samples; do not treat as a brand difference.

source.name: Dirt Rider: How Much Power Does the 2023 Husqvarna FX 450 Make?

statement: Worked out from the same magazine dyno, the 2023 FX 450 made 1.3 hp and 0.8 lb-ft less than the 2023 450 XC-F and peaked 900 rpm higher, despite sharing the engine; the difference is within what unit-to-unit and airbox/exhaust differences can produce.
notes: 53.3-54.6 = -1.3; 32.2-33.0 = -0.8; 10,400-9,500 = +900. Single samples; do not treat as a brand difference.

source.name: Dirt Rider: How Much Power Does the 2023 Husqvarna FX 450 Make?

statement: Testers call the 450 XCF-W the smoothest KTM four-stroke from bottom to top, with no coughing or decel popping; it lugs to very low rpm and finds traction where a motocross bike spins. Peak power sits between the dual-sport and the XC-F.
notes: Tester impression, stock bike. A magazine dyno tester likewise said it builds from the lowest rpm and never feels like too much.

source.name: Dirt Bike Magazine: 2023 KTM 450XCF-W Full Test

statement: On the 2024 XCF-W low rpm is tame, the midrange ramps up strongly and it revs to about 11,000 rpm; torque lets you hold a high gear without bogging. Map 2 is sharp but not abrupt and suits skilled riders.
notes: Tester impression with optional map switch fitted, GNCC-style course.

source.name: Ultimate Motorcycling: 2024 KTM 450 XCF-W Review (GNCC tested)

statement: Testers say the 450 XC-F has as much peak power as any production 450 yet stays manageable, but it stalls more easily than the 350 in tight going and the spinning mass makes it more work at low speed.
notes: Tester impression, stock.

source.name: Dirt Bike Magazine: Riding the 2025 KTM 450XC-F (The Wrap)

statement: Testers describe strong bottom-end pull, a good midrange and more pull on top; it can be ridden like a 450 but rewards revving. In slow, rocky, technical sections the throttle response felt jerky.
notes: 185 lb tester, stock engine, both maps tried.

source.name: Keefer Inc. Testing: 2025 KTM 350 XC-F review

statement: The FX 350 is only about 3 hp short of a 450, pulls a long way, and can be short-shifted when tired; off-road it is ridden lower in the rpm than on a motocross track (mostly under 9,000 rpm), and it stalls less than a 450.
notes: Tester impression.

source.name: Dirt Bike Magazine: 2025 Husqvarna FX350 Full Test

statement: The EX bikes keep the motocross engine character: free-revving with strong mid-to-top pull, but less bottom-end tractability and a less smooth throttle off idle than the EC enduro models.
notes: Tester comparison at the 2024 launch.

source.name: Transmoto: 2024 GasGas Cross-Country Weapons

source.name: Transmoto: 2024 GasGas Cross-Country Weapons

statement: The 2024 FE 450 is smooth and easy to ride with strong low-end grunt and good climbing, pulling from corners in 2nd-4th; it feels heavier and needs more effort in tight sections than the FE 250/350 and sometimes pushed the front.
notes: Australian enduro test; a magazine launch report agrees on weight in slow sections.

source.name: ADB Magazine: Enduro Test 2024 Husqvarna FE 450

statement: The 2021 EX 350F felt weaker than the 350 SX-F and would not pull 3rd cleanly out of a tight uphill turn; testers traced it to the airbox, not the engine.
notes: Tester impression; see engine_mods for the airbox fix.

source.name: Motocross Action: Race Test of the 2021 GasGas EX 350F cross-country

topic: XC-F map switch, traction and launch control
statement: The XC-F has a standard bar switch with two maps (Map 1 more linear, Map 2 sharper throttle response) and a traction control toggle. Launch control is engaged by pressing the traction control and quickshift buttons together, and the quickshifter works 2nd-5th on the 450 (2nd-6th on the 250/350).
notes: QS ranges from a magazine 2024 first look. Map lights: white = map 1, green = map 2.

statement: KTM-group traction control has no wheel-speed sensor. It compares throttle input with how fast engine rpm rises and cuts power when rpm climbs too quickly. It still allows deliberate slides on consistent ground and mainly steps in on slick rock or wet clay; it works with either map, giving four combinations, and keeps its setting after a stall.
notes: Mechanism from the KTM 2026 XCF-W page; behaviour and orange TC light from a magazine 2017 test of the same system.

statement: The Connectivity Unit Offroad bolts behind the number plate with a GPS sensor in the front fender and pairs with the KTMconnect app. It can retrofit 2024-2025 XC-F bikes (standard on 350 XC-F Factory Edition) and adjusts engine braking, throttle response, traction control, launch control and quickshifter, with presets for sand, gravel, hard pack, dry and wet. The rider subscription is 69.99 euro a year; testers put the hardware at about $250.
notes: Hardware price from a magazine 2025 450 XC-F test. KTM does not list the XCF-W as compatible. Numeric parameter ranges not published.

topic: XACT spring fork vs XPLOR on the trail
statement: Testers find the XACT closed-cartridge fork racier: it handles big hits, braking bumps and ruts well but is harsher on roots and loose rock than the EC's XPLOR fork, which in turn is too soft on big hits. The FE 450's switch from XPLOR to XACT made it firmer and less prone to bottoming.
notes: A magazine 2024 EX 350F and FE 450 tests agree.

topic: 350 XC-F tester setup (185 lb, vet B)
statement: A 185 lb vet tester ran the fork 5 clicks out compression, 12 out rebound, tubes at the second line, and the shock at 11 out low-speed compression, 1 turn out high-speed, 12 out rebound with 105 mm sag on stock 14/50 gearing and the green map. For fast desert he suggests dropping the fork to the first line or flush.
notes: Stock springs; tester notes bigger/faster riders need a shock spring and revalve.

topic: Vegas to Reno 450 XC-F desert build

statement: A desert race team ran a 450 XC-F with an added 6th gear, 14/48 gearing (stock 13T front), an FMF slip-on for more bottom-to-mid, a 3.2 gal tank (about 70 fast miles per tank), revalved suspension, 100-110 mm sag and fork air at 135-141 psi.
notes: The bike was a 2019, the same generation as 2020-2022.

statement: Stock settings suit most vet tracks; on faster tracks add at least a few clicks of fork compression, and the rear is usually fine.

statement: The stock soft setting suits WORCS-style racing; desert racers need firmer settings for rocks, and many add a 6th gear because the 5-speed is the bike's main shortcoming for western racing.

notes: In-house dyno (this outlet uses a Dynojet 250i in other tests). 125 SX value DERIVED by subtraction: 36.2-3.0 and 17.1-1.0. rpm figures from dr_tc150tech.

source.name: Dirt Rider - How much power does the 2025 Husqvarna TC 150 make?

statement: The stock TBI 150 SX felt dull at the bottom, strongest in the midrange but flattening, and faded on top so riders short-shifted; the injection tames its two-stroke character toward a four-stroke feel.
notes: Single reviewer.

source.name: Vital MX - FMF Powercore 2.1 and Factory Fatty pipe 2025 KTM 150 SX review

statement: Owners describe the TC 300 as smooth, linear and luggable, smoother than a YZ250; some say it runs out of steam early stock, and a remap is commonly recommended for more over-rev.
notes: Few TC-specific owners in thread.

source.name: Vital MX - 2025 Husqvarna TC300 reviews?

statement: The TBI MC 125 feels more predictable and four-stroke-like with fewer peaks and dips when a shift is missed; the MC 250 has very strong low-end torque and pulls third gear in slow sections.

statement: On a deep, watered sand track an 80 kg tester found the stock 450-RC rear sat high and twitchy on sandy downhills; backing rear preload off a couple of turns to about 40 mm static sag and 102 mm race sag fixed it, with stock clickers. He warned that mid-30s static sag is not enough for this chassis.
notes: Smooth sand track with no chatter, so clickers were not tested. Media launch (Ride Park, Victoria, Australia).

source.name: ADB Magazine: MX Aussie launch Triumph TF 450-RC

topic: 250-X spring choice for a 90 kg rider
statement: A 90 kg tester found the stock springs (built for 70-80 kg) too soft, the medium (80-90 kg) set still a little soft, and the hard (90 kg+) springs let him push properly, with no clicker changes needed.
notes: Soft loamy, well-watered private track (Australia). Spring rates for medium/hard sets not given in N/mm.

source.name: MotoOnline: Tested 2024 Triumph TF 250-X

statement: Testers running 100-102 mm race sag found the stock fork soft: faster riders added 2-3 compression clicks, heavier (190 lb+) vet riders left built-up air in the fork as a temporary stiffener, and lighter riders softened the fork to match the shock. Lowering the fork 3 mm in the clamps calmed a busy front in fast rough corners at some cost to mid-corner precision.
notes: Southern California tracks incl. Perris. Also fitted a 49T rear sprocket (stock 48). 'Leaving air in' means not bleeding the fork caps; it is a temporary fix, not a spring substitute.

source.name: Dirt Bike Test: 2024 Triumph TF 250-X

statement: Compared with the KTM's steel frame and WP air fork, the TF 250-X's aluminium chassis feels livelier and breaks traction a bit more, the spring fork puts more weight on the front, and the bike reacts more to fork height, sag and shock high-speed compression changes. Stock settings suit novice/intermediate riders around 165 lb, and testers ended up near stock clickers.
notes: Paraphrased tester comparison; described as a difference in feel, not a flaw. Also recommends 49T (pro/intermediate) or 50T (novice) rear sprocket and says the 1.85 rear rim can be replaced by 2.15 with a 110 tyre.

source.name: Motocross Action: MXA Race Test 2025 Triumph TF250-X

statement: In a six-bike 250 shootout, testers rated the TF 250-X, with the Honda, as the most flexible (forgiving) chassis in corners, with exceptional handling and corner stability; they found it light and agile.
notes: Spanish shootout (La Farm, Lleida). Frame stiffness not measured; subjective. Same test criticised gearbox effort and quickshift irregularities.

topic: TF 450 recall root cause and revised head
statement: Recall notices cite too little clearance between the exhaust rocker arm and its shaft, which causes excessive friction; the shaft can stiffen or seize. The replacement is a revised complete cylinder head assembly. Germany's authority lists 1,311 bikes worldwide built 13 February to 1 November 2025.
notes: Second-hand report of KBA and Triumph recall wording. North American counts (about 1,560 US + 171 Canada) exceed the KBA worldwide figure; no official explanation. 250 models are not reported as affected.

topic: MX Tune Pro factory maps: engine braking and traction level
statement: Each of Triumph's 10 app maps loads into Map 2 (Map 1 stays full power) with its own engine braking and traction-control level: Novice mid braking/TC 4, Intermediate mid-low/5, Expert low/6, Hard Pack Dry mid-low/4, Hard Pack Wet mid-high/4, Loam Dry mid-low/5, Loam Wet low-mid/5, Sand Dry low-mid/5, Sand Wet minimal/6. OE Factory resets Map 2, traction and launch control to stock.

vals.Novice: smooth power, soft throttle, engine braking mid, GPA 4
vals.Hard Pack Dry: soft power, progressive throttle, mid-low, GPA 4

notes: GPA = Athena traction control. Traction and launch control can be set per map; an LC-GPA accessory switches between race and training mode. Fuel/ignition offsets are shown only as directions (more fuel or less timing at low throttle softens response), no numbers.

topic: traction control range and use in mud
statement: Traction control is adjustable from 1 to 10 in the app. On clay, an off-road tester raised it from the default 3 to 6 with the Soft/Mud map, which limited rear-wheel slip and kept the rear in check; an MX tester found it let him put power down with little slip out of corners.
notes: Range from a magazine AU RC launch test and a magazine 450-C review. Conflicts in tone with tf-050 where MX testers left TC off because it dulled power.

source.name: Ultimate Motorcycling: 2026 Triumph TF 450-C Review

topic: RC Edition holeshot device and map character
statement: The RC Edition's launch control works with a holeshot device fitted only to the RC. A 165 lb tester found the standard full-power map snappy and abrupt off the bottom, while the Carmichael map was more controllable and linear and the Loam-Wet map had the softest hit for mud.
notes: Single-day launch test. Another launch tester called the Carmichael map stronger low down (see conflicts).

source.name: Ultimate Motorcycling: 2025 Triumph TF 450-RC Edition Review

topic: E model traction control and maps in use
statement: On the E models traction control trims wheelspin rather than cutting power; testers recommend the soft map plus traction control in slippery mud, especially on the 450-E. Another tester preferred full-power Map 1 on the 450-E in the wet because traction control kept slip low.
notes: Combined from MOTORRAD and a magazine AU launch tests. One review says the soft-vs-aggressive map difference is noticeable but not extreme (a magazine).

source.name: MOTORRAD: Triumph TF 250-E/450-E erster Fahrtest

topic: E model traction control and maps in use
statement: On the E models traction control trims wheelspin rather than cutting power; testers recommend the soft map plus traction control in slippery mud, especially on the 450-E. Another tester preferred full-power Map 1 on the 450-E in the wet because traction control kept slip low.
notes: Combined from MOTORRAD and a magazine AU launch tests. One review says the soft-vs-aggressive map difference is noticeable but not extreme (a magazine).

source.name: MOTORRAD: Triumph TF 250-E/450-E erster Fahrtest

statement: Testers found the E models' upshift quickshifter works best at high revs and full throttle; under hard acceleration it sometimes failed to engage the next gear, though it helped on hill climbs.
notes: A magazine and MOTORRAD agree on high-rpm preference; a magazine AU found it useful on climbs.

source.name: 1000PS: Triumph TF 250-E and TF 450-E Review 2025

statement: Testers found the E models' upshift quickshifter works best at high revs and full throttle; under hard acceleration it sometimes failed to engage the next gear, though it helped on hill climbs.
notes: A magazine and MOTORRAD agree on high-rpm preference; a magazine AU found it useful on climbs.

source.name: 1000PS: Triumph TF 250-E and TF 450-E Review 2025

topic: 250-E feel on climbs and low revs
statement: The 250-E pulls smoothly from low revs without stalling or popping, has a strong midrange and keeps revving on top; on long steep climbs one tester needed a couple of stops where the 450-E went up easily.
notes: Claims as printed by a magazine AU; feel from MOTORRAD and a magazine AU.

source.name: MOTORRAD: Triumph TF 250-E/450-E erster Fahrtest

statement: Testers describe the 450-E as responding early, softly and precisely, with linear delivery and flywheel momentum that make it feel light, closer to a 350, yet able to punch hard when asked.
notes: Claimed figures vary by outlet (see conflicts).

source.name: MOTORRAD: Triumph TF 250-E/450-E erster Fahrtest

statement: A 180 lb tester in fast, clay woods used the Soft/Mud map with traction control at 6, 102 mm rear race sag with stock clickers, and Dunlop Geomax AT82 tyres at 12 psi front / 11 psi rear; the fork resisted bottoming on fast drop-offs and the shock used full stroke.
notes: Stock C additions: 2.2 gal tank, flag hand guards, plastic skid plate with linkage guard, tool-less filter access, kickstand, 18-inch rear.

source.name: Ultimate Motorcycling: 2026 Triumph TF 450-C Review

statement: One launch test found the E baseline firm but not harsh, suiting light fast riders or heavier slower ones, and praised the KYB fork's sensitivity and progression; another found the 450-E fork set soft enough to reach its limits on rough ground.
notes: MOTORRAD (firm baseline) vs a magazine (soft 450-E fork); tf-073 also reports fork diving on the 450-E.

source.name: MOTORRAD: Triumph TF 250-E/450-E erster Fahrtest

statement: One launch test found the E baseline firm but not harsh, suiting light fast riders or heavier slower ones, and praised the KYB fork's sensitivity and progression; another found the 450-E fork set soft enough to reach its limits on rough ground.

source.name: MOTORRAD: Triumph TF 250-E/450-E erster Fahrtest

statement: One launch test rated the E clutch excellent, able to lug the 250-E up a hill with one finger; another earlier test noted a heavy clutch pull. Neutral-finding and shifting were rated only passable.
notes: Conflicts with tf-083 (heavy pull).

statement: One long-term tester found the 450-RC stock clutch light and vague with weak bite, and reported stock plates lasting about 10 hours; an aftermarket plate and stiffer spring kit gave a firmer pull and more engagement feel.
notes: Single tester; 2026 450-X got a higher-capacity Exedy hub and new Belleville spring (tf-005).

source.name: Keefer Inc. Testing: Hinson clutch pack for Triumph TF-450 RC Edition

statement: Beyond the valve guides, clutch and shift drum changes already noted, the 2027 TF 250-X adds Neken 7075-T6 triple clamps for front feel, tool-free clicker adjustment, a reworked chain guide and fork guards and a relocated start-stop switch; claimed power stays 48 hp at 13,500 rpm.
notes: Context for 2026 owners: the new clamps and drum may retrofit, unconfirmed.

source.name: 1000PS: Triumph TF 250-X 2027 updates from the MX2 World Championship

topic: 2026 MX2 world title and factory electronics
statement: Triumph Factory Racing won the 2026 FIM MX2 world title with Guillem Farres (Camden McLellan second) plus the MX2 manufacturers' title. The GP team runs Motec electronics, while the US team uses Athena GET electronics with its own GET display.
notes: Electronics detail from a magazine Pit Bits, 2026 Motocross of Nations. No published factory-vs-production engine or suspension spec found.

source.name: Powersports Business: Triumph takes home its first-ever MX2 World Championship

statement: One experienced tester set the shock to 102 mm race sag with high-speed compression 7/8 turn out to lift the rear under throttle, raised the fork 3 mm and went 2 clicks stiffer on fork compression to balance the bike; he ran the Pirelli tyres at 14 psi and would fit a 110 rear.
notes: Tester notes the shock needs more end-stroke damping (adding high-speed compression helps).

source.name: PulpMX: Triumph TF 250-X test notes (Keefer)

statement: The 250-X tends to stand up mid-corner in tight turns, which one tester puts down partly to the 100-section rear tyre and partly to stiffness around the head tube and clamps; the stock Pirelli MX32 carcass wears out before the knobs and then rolls under load.

source.name: PulpMX: Triumph TF 250-X test notes (Keefer)

statement: Owner reports are mixed: one rider had repeated stalls (once off a jump face) even after raising idle; owners complain about stock tyres and hard-to-find aftermarket parts; two to three riders felt the engine goes flat on top while two others rated its low end close to a 2024 YZ250F.
notes: Small sample, late 2024; some impressions from demo rides.

source.name: Vital MX forum: Triumph TF250X worth it?

statement: Owner reports are mixed: one rider had repeated stalls (once off a jump face) even after raising idle; owners complain about stock tyres and hard-to-find aftermarket parts; two to three riders felt the engine goes flat on top while two others rated its low end close to a 2024 YZ250F.
notes: Small sample, late 2024; some impressions from demo rides.

source.name: Vital MX forum: Triumph TF250X worth it?

statement: Two of two owners who posted changed the 450's gearing (13/50 with 116-link chain; 13/52 with two extra links and axle back), and favoured sand-oriented maps (Sand-Wet or a deep-sand map) with Expert or the RC map suggested; a 240 lb owner fitted 0.52 kg/mm fork springs.
notes: Supplements tf-075.

statement: A 165 lb tester ran stock clickers and 100 mm sag; he found the fork a little soft on jump landings and the front pushing in corners, and suggested adding fork compression clicks and raising the fork 1-2 mm. Carmichael himself runs the fork 6 mm up and wanted 7 mm.
notes: Single day of testing.

statement: In one 2026 seven-bike 250 shootout the TF 250-X finished fourth, the same place as the year before; the magazine judged the 2026 changes not enough to move it up.
notes: Article body (dyno, weights) not readable; only the summary.

source.name: Dirt Rider: Best Motocross Bike 4th Place - 2026 Triumph TF 250-X

statement: For 2020 the CRF450R got the battery 28 mm lower in a new airbox (better filter airflow), fork valving revised to ride higher, three-level Honda Selectable Torque Control (traction control) on the bar, new rear brake pads and a revised rear rotor guard; the engine was nearly unchanged apart from mapping.
notes: Honda changes as reported by magazines; a magazine says the rotor guard was redesigned for cooling, a magazine says removed.

source.name: Motocross Action: MXA Race Test 2020 Honda CRF450

statement: On a magazine in-house Dynojet rear-wheel dyno the 2020 CRF450R made 53.3 hp at 9,800 rpm and 32.2 lb-ft at 6,900 rpm.
notes: A magazine Dynojet; stock; map not stated.

source.name: Dirt Rider: 2020 Honda CRF450R Dyno Test

statement: On a Dynojet at an exhaust maker's shop in a 2020 450 shootout the CRF450R made 56.63 hp at 9,700 rpm and 34.28 lb-ft at 7,200 rpm, more than the KX450 on the same day.
notes: Bikes run back to back on FMF's Dynojet; stock.

source.name: Vital MX: 2020 450 Shootout full test

statement: On another magazine's dyno the 2020 CRF450R peaked at 59.74 hp at 9,600 rpm against 60.21 hp at 9,500 rpm for the 2019, which made more power at almost every point up to the 11,600 rpm sign-off; the 2020 led only above about 9,600 rpm and was still the most powerful 450 of 2020.
notes: A magazine dyno, type not stated. Below 9,600 rpm the KTM 450 SX-F made more.

source.name: Motocross Action: MXA Race Test 2020 Honda CRF450

statement: Measured weights for the 2020 CRF450R: 238 lb without fuel (same as 2018-2019) on one scale and 247.9 lb with a full tank on another.
notes: Full-tank figure from a magazine 2020 450 shootout scale.

source.name: Motocross Action: MXA Race Test 2020 Honda CRF450

statement: Testers found the 2020 CRF450R 'stagey' low down (snappy, then calm, then revvy) with a very strong midrange that lugs third gear in slow turns; broader and less scary than the 2019 but still the hardest-hitting 450 of its year, which some riders found abrupt on rough tracks.
notes: magazines shootout testers agree it was the strongest/most aggressive 2020 450.

source.name: Motocross Action: MXA Race Test 2020 Honda CRF450

statement: HSTC level 1 is the least intrusive and level 3 the most; it acts only when the rear spins. One tester found level 1 worked well on slippery hardpack while levels 2-3 held the bike back, and liked the aggressive map with HSTC 1; another magazine found the aggressive map crisper but about 1 hp down everywhere.
notes: magazines.

source.name: ADB: 2020 Honda CRF450R review

statement: Launch control has three rev-limit levels rather than retarding ignition, and is armed through the starter button; some testers used traction control instead for starts.

source.name: Motocross Action: MXA Race Test 2020 Honda CRF450

statement: Magazine race setup: fork 5.0 N/mm, compression 6 out (pro) / 12 (intermediate) / 13 (vet), rebound 10 out (stock 12), flush; shock 56 N/mm, 107 mm race sag, high-speed 2 3/4 turns out (stock 3), low-speed 10 out (stock 9), rebound 7 out (stock 9). Stock 13/49 gearing is close; some ran 13/48.
notes: One 240 lb shootout tester ran 105 mm sag and moved the fork 2 mm to balance a shock that overpowered the fork (a magazine).

source.name: Motocross Action: MXA Race Test 2020 Honda CRF450

statement: Known 2020 complaints: weak clutch with a judder spring (fix: remove it and add a full-size friction plate), radiator boil-over (higher-pressure cap), soft fork bottoming on landings, shock harsh on square edges, an inconsistent rough-track feel, and 117.5 dB on the 2-metre max sound test (115 dB limit).
notes: No 2020 CRF450R recall found; Honda's drive-chain recall (CPSC 21-741) covers 2021 only.

source.name: Motocross Action: MXA Race Test 2020 Honda CRF450

statement: Race-prepped for a desert GP, a 2020 CRF450RX got a 14-tooth countershaft (stock 13), a 2.4 gal tank (stock 2.2 gal), heavy-duty tubes, standard map and HSTC level 2; stock clickers worked for a heavier tester at about 118 mm sag, with one hard fork bottoming.
notes: Mild map too soft for fast course; aggressive map strong bottom but lost top. Two flats despite heavy-duty tubes.

source.name: Dirt Bike Magazine: 2020 Honda CRF450RX first ride (Ridgecrest GP)

statement: On a magazine in-house rear-wheel dyno the 2020 CRF250RX made 38.2 hp at 11,900 rpm and 17.9 lb-ft at 9,300 rpm.
notes: A magazine in-house dyno (same outlet's CRF250R test used a Dynojet: 39.4 hp @ 12,300).

source.name: Dirt Rider: 2020 Honda CRF250RX Dyno Test

statement: The 2020 CRF250RX shares the R's 2020 engine changes (later exhaust cam, new chamber, per-gear ignition) but has a 2.25 gal tank vs 1.6, an 18-inch rear wheel, O-ring chain, kickstand, softer suspension and softer standard map; its Map 3 equals the MX bike's standard map. For 2020 it also got a taller second gear and a clutch with 18% more friction area and stiffer springs.
notes: Honda changes as reported by a magazine; it also mentions a less rigid frame and swingarm, larger filter and left radiator.

source.name: Dirt Bike Magazine: 2020 Honda CRF250RX full test

statement: Weighed without fuel the 2020 CRF250RX was 235 lb, about 8 lb more than the MX bike. Power is smooth and linear; low end is better than 2019 but still weak, so it must be revved. Map 2 softens the top without adding bottom; Map 3 adds top end.
notes: An aftermarket exhaust added some low end (no dyno).

source.name: Dirt Bike Magazine: 2020 Honda CRF250RX full test

statement: Testers noted the RX runs hot with boil-over risk on warm days with heavy clutch use, and in a muddy race the clutch faded badly and the bike stalled a few times; it has no stock spark arrestors and a full tank makes it feel top-heavy.
notes: magazines.

source.name: Cycle News: 2020 Honda CRF250RX Review

statement: The 2020 KX450 was mechanically unchanged from the all-new 2019 bike; only graphics changed, and the 2019 bike's weak points carried over.
notes: Confirmed by a magazine ('no mechanical changes for 2020').

source.name: Motocross Action: MXA Race Test 2020 Kawasaki KX450

statement: On a magazine in-house rear-wheel dyno the 2020 KX450 made 51.9 hp at 9,200 rpm and 32.9 lb-ft at 6,800 rpm.
notes: A magazine (Dynojet-equipped outlet; type not restated on page); stock, green coupler assumed.

source.name: Dirt Rider: 2020 Kawasaki KX450 Dyno Test

statement: On a Dynojet in a 2020 450 shootout the KX450 made 54.71 hp at 9,400 rpm and 33.87 lb-ft at 7,100 rpm.
notes: Same dyno/day as CRF450R 56.63 hp.

source.name: Vital MX: 2020 450 Shootout full test

statement: On another magazine dyno the 2020 KX450 peaked at 55.8 hp at 9,500 rpm, against 56.4 hp at 8,800 rpm for the 2018 KX450F, which made about 1.5 lb-ft more torque from 5,000 to 9,400 rpm; about 4 hp less than the 2020 CRF450R.
notes: A magazine dyno, type not stated.

source.name: Motocross Action: MXA Race Test 2020 Kawasaki KX450

statement: Weighed without fuel the 2020 KX450 was 233 lb (lightest Japanese 450 of 2020; 242.8 lb full tank on another scale). Testers describe a quick-hitting, fast-revving bottom, steady midrange build and a strong surge above about 9,400 rpm: throttle response over peak power.
notes: Full-tank weight from a magazine shootout.

source.name: Motocross Action: MXA Race Test 2020 Kawasaki KX450

statement: Green (stock) coupler is the best all-round map; black is softer and loses about 1-2 hp from 6,000 to 11,500 rpm; white is crisper with the same peak. Custom maps loaded with Kawasaki's calibration tool override the coupler.
notes: Magazine's own maps advance midrange-up ignition and richen midrange fuel.

source.name: Motocross Action: MXA Race Test 2020 Kawasaki KX450

statement: Magazine race setup: fork 5.1 N/mm (one 5.2 and one 5.0 spring; 5.0 light, 5.2 fast riders), compression 14 out, rebound 12 out, 2 mm up (flush on stock springs); shock 54 N/mm (52 for riders under 150 lb), high-speed 1 1/4 turns out, low-speed 18 out, rebound 12 out, 105 mm race sag.
notes: Light riders: add fork oil in 5 cc steps to cut bottoming.

source.name: Motocross Action: MXA Race Test 2020 Kawasaki KX450

statement: Known 2020 KX450 issues: touchy rear brake that locks on corner entry (chamfer pads, shorten master-cylinder rod), overheating in heat/sand/long motos (2.0 kg/cm2 radiator cap), soft fork for fast riders, fast clutch-plate wear and incomplete disengagement, quick-wearing lower chain roller and guide, and cracking fork guards.
notes: A magazine shootout testers also named the soft fork as the main complaint (3rd of 7 overall).

source.name: Motocross Action: MXA Race Test 2020 Kawasaki KX450

statement: The 2020 KX250 got a reworked engine: bore/stroke 78.0 x 52.2 mm (was 77.0 x 53.6), compression 14.2:1 (was 13.4), finger-follower valvetrain, 32 mm intake / 26.5 mm exhaust valves (was 31/25), 44 mm throttle body (was 43), relocated injectors, airbox vents on both sides and a 30 mm shorter header. Showa SFF fork and shock were replaced by a KYB 48 mm coil fork and KYB shock with a longer link, and the rear rotor grew to 250 mm.
notes: Kawasaki specs as reported by magazines (also ~5% stiffer effective spring rates, reshaped engine mounts). No electric start until 2021.

source.name: Motocross Action: MXA Race Test 2020 Kawasaki KX250

topic: 2020 KX250 bore/stroke ratio and piston speed
statement: Worked out from 78.0 x 52.2 mm, the 2020 KX250 is 1.49:1 oversquare, and mean piston speed at the roughly 13,500 rpm rev ceiling is about 23.5 m/s.

source.name: BAK MX calculation from published bore/stroke

statement: Testers found the 2020 KX250 weaker down low than the 2019 but much stronger on top, pulling right to its roughly 13,500 rpm ceiling instead of flattening at 10,000; it matched a YZ250F on top but exited corners slower. It weighed 223 lb without fuel.
notes: Weight a magazine scale; feel from magazines.

source.name: Dirt Bike Magazine: 2020 Kawasaki KX250 full test

statement: Pros preferred the white (aggressive) coupler, vets and novices the green (standard); the black (mild) made the soft low end softer and none raised the rev ceiling. Launch control was seen as little use because the engine lacks bottom power.

source.name: Motocross Action: MXA Race Test 2020 Kawasaki KX250

statement: Magazine race setup: fork 5.0 N/mm (4.8 or 4.4 for light riders), compression 13 out, rebound 10 out, standard height (2 mm up if it stands up mid-corner); shock 54 N/mm, high-speed 1.5 turns out, low-speed 7 out, rebound 17 out, 105 mm race sag. Stock 50-tooth rear; most went to 51, 49 for tight hardpack.
notes: Another magazine ran about 100 mm sag (vs 106 mm recommended) to help the front bite (a magazine).

source.name: Motocross Action: MXA Race Test 2020 Kawasaki KX250

statement: 2020 KX250 issues: no electric start and hard hot starting (7-8 kicks), fast clutch wear, chain guide worn out in about 15 hours, a harsh spot about three-quarters into fork travel, close shift points, and extra noise with both airbox vents open.

statement: Testers found the 2024 250 snappy right off idle but prone to a bog on a hard throttle snap, then a surge and a dip into the mid; the main power comes in the upper mid to lower top, and it signs off earlier than a KTM, with riders bouncing off the limiter. Low-end and mid were rated its weakest areas against Honda and KTM.
notes: Consistent across a magazine, a magazine Test and a magazine. Why: lean throttle-snap mapping (a magazine calls it mapping, not electrical), tall 13/48 gearing and wide 2-3 and 3-4 gaps.

statement: Testers describe the 450 as smooth and linear rather than a brute: slightly soft off the bottom in the standard map, a strong midrange, and a top end that tapers or signs off early, with nothing gained by over-revving. It is milder than a Yamaha or KTM and feels closer to a Honda, Kawasaki or Suzuki; it works best shifted earlier than most 450s.
notes: A magazine RC and X; a magazine compares it to a CRF450R/KX. Why: long 63.4 mm stroke, smooth mapping and tall gearing; a smooth curve feels slower than its dyno peak, so riders rated it mid-pack for power despite top-3 dyno numbers.

topic: power valve calibration after top-end work
statement: The electronic power valve must be re-taught its end stops after the cylinder is removed: plug in the brand's wake-up dongle with throttle held at half for 10 seconds, then release so the valve cycles. Skipping it can make the bike bog or not rev.
notes: Procedure as described by a magazine from dealer practice; each brand (KTM/Husqvarna/GasGas) uses its own dongle.

source.name: ADB Magazine - How to reset a KTM TBI power valve

topic: power valve preload screw - direction and feel
statement: Turning the preload screw clockwise (in) gives smoother power and broader bottom end; counterclockwise (out) gives more hit and maximum top end. Adjust in 1/8 turns; total range is six turns.
notes: CONFLICT on direction: a magazine 'This much we know' and a magazine say one turn out opens the valve 150 rpm sooner (smoother) and in opens later (more hit), the opposite of a magazine Ask the MXperts text. See conflicts. Do not loosen the two screws holding the brass adjuster body.

statement: Stock TBI mapping is conservative and runs flat into the rev limiter; a tuner remap kept the easy bottom end, added throttle response and mid-to-top pull, and reduced limiter hits. Pipe-specific maps exist (FMF, a tuner, DR.D).
notes: No dyno numbers published. A tester (2023 300SX) described stock as rich and lethargic and the remap as adding low-rpm response and 2nd/3rd gear pull. Tuners such as WMR and Jamie Ellis cracked the locked ECU.

statement: The YZ250 power valve is driven by a crank-gear centrifugal governor and has three pieces: a center valve that opens in the first half of control-rod rotation and two side valves that open in the second half, held by torsion springs that default it closed.
notes: Description from US patent 9,797,275 (aftermarket inventor describing the stock 1999-on design). The patent attributes the YZ250's mid-rpm 'hit' to the center valve reaching its stop, where friction and spring force cause hesitation then surge.

statement: Yamaha softened the YZ250X by raising head volume from 21.5 to 23.6 cc (compression 8.9 to 7.9:1), raising the exhaust port 0.5 mm with a matching valve shape, retarding the CDI in the mid-to-high range, and setting the governor spring/preload to open the valve sooner; the pipe is 35 mm narrower.
notes: Yamaha changes as reported by a magazine. Result: milder hit, tractable to 6,500 rpm, dip at 7,000 picking up at 7,400, same peak around 8,800 rpm, more over-rev. A real-world example of how head volume, port height, ignition and PV timing move a two-stroke's power.

statement: A port open for a fixed number of crank degrees is open for less time as rpm rises: time = degrees / (6 x rpm). A 190-degree exhaust port is open 3.7 ms at 8,600 rpm but 7.9 ms at 4,000 rpm, which is why a tall port suits high rpm and wastes charge at low rpm.
notes: t = theta/(6N): 190/(6*8600) = 0.00368 s; 190/(6*4000) = 0.00792 s. Formula from Jennings 1964. 190 deg is an illustrative duration, not a measured figure for any bike here.

source.name: Cycle World - Tuned exhaust for the two-stroke (Gordon H. Jennings)

notes: t = theta/(6N): 190/(6*8600) = 0.00368 s; 190/(6*4000) = 0.00792 s. Formula from Jennings 1964. 190 deg is an illustrative duration, not a measured figure for any bike here.

statement: Jennings' handbook sizes ports by time-area (port area x open time per cc of swept volume): about 0.00014-0.00015 s-cm2/cm3 for exhaust, 0.00008-0.00010 for transfers and 0.00014-0.00016 for piston-port intake. Motocross engines run less exhaust and more transfer time-area than road racers for smoother power.
notes: Second-hand summary of Gordon Jennings, Two-Stroke Tuner's Handbook (1973). Specific time-area = mean port area x (degrees/(6N)) / swept volume.

topic: principle - raise vs widen the exhaust port
statement: Raising the exhaust port opens it earlier, adding duration and time-area: peak power moves up the rpm range but the band narrows and bottom end is lost. Widening adds area without adding duration, so it gains top end while keeping the band broader.
notes: Jennings via summary; dt125r tuner thread (Calum) also notes raising the barrel lowers trapped compression and changes every port's timing, so it needs head and ignition rework. Yamaha's YZ250X (+0.5 mm exhaust plus lower compression) gains over-rev and loses hit.
